structure.title: Act I · The court and the wrestling ground
structure.text: Orlando's elder brother withholds the education their father intended for him. Rosalind lives under the protection of the uncle who displaced her father. A wrestling match brings the pair together just before both households become unsafe.

structure.title: Act II – Act III, scene 4 · Arden · How to live outside the court
structure.text: Exiles need food and shelter in a forest already occupied by working shepherds. Rosalind, travelling as the boy Ganymede, meets Orlando hanging verses on trees. The disguise gives her an unusual opportunity to hear her lover practise loving her.

structure.title: Act III, scene 5 – epilogue · Courtships converge
structure.text: A shepherdess takes an interest in the wrong person. Other couples have quite different ideas of what getting married involves. Rosalind undertakes to arrange a meeting whose success depends on managing several promises and one well-kept secret.

people.name: Rosalind and Celia
people.text: Celia chooses to accompany the banished Rosalind. Their ease in teasing and correcting each other gives the audience an intimacy older than the romance and a companion who knows what the disguise conceals.

people.name: Touchstone and Jaques
people.role: A fool and a melancholy observer
people.text: Each enjoys finding folly in other people's enthusiasms. The professional fool proving a point to a shepherd and the melancholy gentleman turning a meeting into a speech can be as funny as their targets.

context.title: Country life has a price
context.text: Court exiles find freedom in the forest. A shepherd who works somebody else's farm has less freedom to offer hospitality than a newcomer expects. The play keeps several experiences of country life within earshot.

notice.text: What sort of cure does Ganymede prescribe?
notice.why: Rosalind offers to cure Orlando by having him court her as though she were Rosalind. A rehearsal lets her ask questions she could scarcely put to him openly, and gives both of them practice in answering.

notice.text: Listen to the replies after the speeches.
notice.why: A polished observation about all humanity often meets a more practical person with an immediate need. The next line can change the standing of a line famous enough to quote on its own.

opening: Banished from court, Rosalind enters the forest dressed as a young man and meets the man she loves. He does not recognise her. She offers to cure his infatuation by pretending to be Rosalind, an arrangement that gives her extraordinary freedom to discover what he expects from a woman. Around them, exiles, shepherds, and fools try out ways of living beyond the court's rules. Shakespeare makes falling in love funny enough to expose the habits that declarations of eternal devotion tend to conceal.
